name: California

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 31st through 38th Congresses (1849–1865), California elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: Statehood
events.text: California became the 31st state on September 9, 1850. Congress gave it 2 seats in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, California kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, California's House delegation grew from 2 to 3 seats.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, California's House delegation grew from 3 to 4 seats.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, California's House delegation grew from 4 to 6 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 48th Congress (1883–1885), California elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, California's House delegation grew from 6 to 7 seats.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, California's House delegation grew from 7 to 8 seats.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, California's House delegation grew from 8 to 11 seats.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, California's House delegation grew from 11 to 20 seats.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, California's House delegation grew from 20 to 23 seats.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, California's House delegation grew from 23 to 30 seats.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, California's House delegation grew from 30 to 38 seats.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, California's House delegation grew from 38 to 43 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, California's House delegation grew from 43 to 45 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, California's House delegation grew from 45 to 52 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, California's House delegation grew from 52 to 53 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Citizens commission draws congressional maps
events.text: California voters approved Proposition 20, giving the Citizens Redistricting Commission the job of drawing congressional districts. Its first congressional map was used from the 2012 election.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, California kept 53 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, California's House delegation shrank from 53 to 52 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Proposition 50
events.text: In a November 4, 2025 special election, voters approved Proposition 50, replacing the commission-drawn congressional map with one drawn by the legislature for the 2026, 2028 and 2030 elections. A three-judge federal court upheld it in January 2026, the Supreme Court declined to block it in February, and it was used in the 2026 election.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c039.text: New map drawn after the 1860 census, which raised California's seats from 2 to 3. It was first used in the 1864 election.

c040.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c043.text: New map drawn after the 1870 census, which raised California's seats from 3 to 4. It was first used in the 1872 election.

c049.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which raised California's seats from 4 to 6. It was first used in the 1884 election.

c053.text: New map drawn after the 1890 census, which raised California's seats from 6 to 7. It was first used in the 1892 election.

c058.text: New map drawn after the 1900 census, which raised California's seats from 7 to 8. It was first used in the 1902 election.

c063.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which raised California's seats from 8 to 11. It was first used in the 1912 election.

c073.text: New map drawn after the 1930 census, which raised California's seats from 11 to 20. It was first used in the 1932 election.

c078.text: New map drawn after the 1940 census, which raised California's seats from 20 to 23. It was first used in the 1942 election.

c083.text: New map drawn after the 1950 census, which raised California's seats from 23 to 30. It was first used in the 1952 election.

c088.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which raised California's seats from 30 to 38. It was first used in the 1962 election.

c091.text: In Silver v. Reagan (1967) the California Supreme Court ordered the Legislature to redraw the 1961 districts to equalize population. The Legislature passed a new map in a late-1967 special session, and the court upheld it for the 1968 elections.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which raised California's seats from 38 to 43. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c094.text: After the Legislature and Governor did not agree on a post-1970 plan, the California Supreme Court appointed special masters. In Legislature v. Reinecke (1973) it adopted their plans, including 43 congressional districts, which were first used in 1974.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised California's seats from 43 to 45. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c099.text: Voters rejected the 1981 congressional plan by referendum in June 1982, though it was used for that year's election. The Legislature then enacted replacement districts in its 1983-84 First Extraordinary Session; the state supreme court barred a 1983 initiative that would have redrawn them again.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which raised California's seats from 45 to 52. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which raised California's seats from 52 to 53. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which left California with 53 seats. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: California's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 2016 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which cut California's seats from 53 to 52. It was first used in the 2022 election.

c120.text: New map following: Proposition 50. In a November 4, 2025 special election, voters approved Proposition 50, replacing the commission-drawn congressional map with one drawn by the legislature for the 2026, 2028 and 2030 elections. A three-judge federal court upheld it in January 2026, the Supreme Court declined to block it in February, and it was used in the 2026 election.
